articles.title: Torfaen becomes global hotspot for carbon emissions after wildfires
articles.summary: The smell of burning from the Blaenavon wildfire was reported 30 miles away in Cardiff.
articles.body:
A county in Wales had one of the world's highest carbon emissions per square kilometre due to wildfires in July, according to a charity.

The fire above Blaenavon, Torfaen was described as "one of the largest and most challenging" in south Wales in recent years by the fire service.

Save the Children said it was concerned about possible health consequences after data published by the European Union's earth observation programme, Copernicus, showed Torfaen behind Malanje in Angola, Spain's Ávila and Annaba in Algeria in terms of wildfire emissions in July.

Torfaen council said it was unaware of the EU data but its own air quality monitoring showed "elevated particulate concentrations".

A blaze the size of about 300 football pitches broke out on Mynydd Garnclochdy, between Abersychan and Blaenavon, with people reporting smelling smoke about 30 (48km) miles away in Cardiff.

Combined with others across the region it contributed to a major incident being declared , which eventually required assistance from the military .

Blaenavon councillor Janet Jones said the smoke had been "particularly bad" on 13 August - about three weeks after the fire first ignited.

"There was great concern about air quality and the impact on elderly people and those suffering with respiratory issues such as emphysema and COPD."

Jones said she had spoken with GP practice nurses two weeks ago and was not aware of any increase in patients complaining about respiratory problems, but added this "could change in the months ahead".

Melanie Simmonds, head of Save the Children Wales, said: "In Wales and across the world, children are breathing in smoke from wildfires, coping with extreme heat and losing the freedom to play outdoors because the air is no longer safe.

"These conditions are not only frightening - they carry serious health consequences for children whose bodies and lungs are still developing."

Torfaen council said it was not aware of the research and "it is not clear what data or evidence was used in the assessment to arrive at the reported conclusion".

It said it "recognises that prolonged wildfire incidents have the potential to adversely affect local air quality, particularly through increased levels of smoke and particulate matter".

It added it "continuously monitors" air quality through a monitoring station in Croesyceiliog Cwmbran.

"While elevated particulate concentrations have been observed during the wildfire period, the council's monitoring station is intended to provide information on general background air quality rather than conditions at specific locations immediately adjacent to the fires," it said.

The Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS) website said it was part of European Union's Space programme, and provided global information related to air pollution and health.

Its data said emissions in Torfaen had been "extremely unusual".

articles.title: Belgian car salesman becomes prince after DNA test proves royal parentage
articles.summary: A car salesman has formally become a prince at the age of 26 after being formally acknowledged as the son of the Belgian King’s brother Prince Laurent.
articles.body: A Belgian car salesman has become a prince at the age of 26 after being acknowledged as the son of the king’s brother, Prince Laurent. Clément Vandenkerckhove’s mother, a Belgian singer who had a relationship with Prince Laurent in the 1990s, only told him who his father was when he turned 16 a decade ago. It emerged this week that he was legally recognized as the son and heir of the 63-year-old younger brother of King Philippe, at a low-key town hall ceremony about six months ago after a DNA test proved his link to the royal family. Prince Laurent has registered his paternity of Vandenkerckhove with Belgium’s civil registry, The Telegraph reported on Wednesday. The formality affords the new prince equal inheritance rights to Laurent’s private estate with his half-sister Princess Louise, 20, and half-brothers Prince Nicolas, 20, and Prince Aymeric, 19, children Laurent shares with Princess Claire whom he married in 2003. But he will not receive a royal allowance, nor will he be expected to take on official duties, and he has no rights to the Belgian throne. Vandenkerckhove could take his father’s family name, Saxe-Coburg, but has indicated he may not choose to. “I am proud of the name Vandenkerckhove,” he recently told Flemish daily newspaper Het Nieuwsblad. “If I were to sacrifice that family name, it would be a betrayal of everything my mother has done for me.” Vandenkerckhove was born in August 2000 to Belgian singer Wendy Van Wanten, whose real name is Iris Vandenkerckhove. She and Laurent dated in the 1990s after a chance encounter at a fashion show in Paris but the relationship did not last and there has been speculation that Laurent’s father, the former king, disapproved. In a documentary that aired on Belgian network VTM last September, Vandenkerckhove recounted his mother’s admission that Laurent was his father. Four years after that, he contacted his father to share what he’d been told and Prince Laurent agreed to a DNA test. “We went to the hospital together and I remember him saying, ‘I’ll go first so you’re feeling at ease,’” Vandenkerckhove told VTM. Once paternity was confirmed, Vandenkerckhove said he and his father had engaged in “open and honest conversations.” This is not the first time a secret involving Belgium’s Royal Family has emerged. Laurent’s father, now 92, fought a paternity battle for many years before admitting in 2020 that he had fathered a daughter during an affair. Delphine Boël, 58, eventually won her legal fight and was granted the title of princess. She now uses the name Delphine de Saxe-Coburg.

Prince Laurent (right) dated Wendy Van Wanten (left), mother of Vandenkerckhove, during the 1990s.

articles.title: From fondue to casseroles: Classic 1960s foods that defined a generation
articles.summary: From fondue at the 1964 World's Fair to Julia Child's "The French Chef," these midcentury dishes defined American home cooking in the 1960s and '70s.
articles.body: The 1960s marked a shift in American cuisine as international dishes gained popularity, while the processed and convenience foods of the 1950s remained staples on dinner tables. C. A. Swanson & Sons introduced the frozen TV dinner in 1954, "marketing it as an easy-to-prepare, fun-to-eat meal, with a disposable tray that reduced cleanup time," the Smithsonian National Museum of American History reported. "The portable TV dinner tapped into middle-class Americans' excitement over television, allowing families to eat in front of their new sets." VINTAGE PHOTOS REVEAL WHAT GROCERY SHOPPING LOOKED LIKE IN THE 1960s Julia Child's first television cooking show, "The French Chef," debuted in 1963, and with it came a new approach to preparing foreign fare for middle-class home cooks. Do you remember eating the following classic dishes during the midcentury? Fondue The Swiss tradition of fondue took America by storm in the 1960s and ‘70s, thanks in part to the Swiss Pavilion serving Swiss cheese fondue at the 1964 New York World's Fair. Fondue is derived from the French word fondre, which means "to melt."  The dish involves melting cheese, wine and seasonings together in a pot and eating it communally with bread, meat and other items. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS Fondue sets became a fashionable centerpiece of entertaining during the '60s and '70s. Casseroles As convenience cooking grew in popularity during the midcentury, casseroles incorporating canned and processed products fit the bill. Green bean casserole was created by Campbell's test kitchen employee Dorcas Reilly in 1955 and was originally called "Green Bean Bake," according to the company's website. "To this day, the recipe calls for only six ingredients: canned or fresh green beans, Campbell's Cream of Mushroom soup, soy sauce, black pepper, milk and French-fried onions," the website says. A recipe for tuna, noodle and mushroom soup casserole was included in the 1951 version of "The Joy of Cooking." CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER Chicken divan, a casserole combining chicken and broccoli in a creamy sauce and often topped with cheese and breadcrumbs, was another popular dish of the era. Chicken Kiev The exact origins of chicken Kiev are disputed, but it has connections to French culinary techniques and Eastern European cuisine, Tasting Table reported.  It is made by stuffing a chicken breast with cold, garlic-and-herb butter, breading the chicken and frying it. Frozen versions of this item are available in grocery stores today. French Onion Dip Lipton's introduced its dehydrated onion soup in the early 1950s.  By the middle of the decade, home cooks were combining it with sour cream to make what became known as California dip, later called French onion dip, a go-to snack item and party food, according to the website Quaint Cooking. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ The dip has evolved from the original, two-ingredient recipe.  Modern iterations of it involve using Greek yogurt, whipped cottage cheese or cream cheese. Other retro food favorites that baby boomers may remember fondly include Swedish meatballs, chicken à la king and grasshopper pie. Swedish meatballs are typically made with a meat mixture, breadcrumbs and egg and topped with gravy. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Chicken à la king uses chicken, vegetables and a cream sauce and is typically served over toast, rice or noodles. Grasshopper pie is a no-bake dessert that incorporates crème de menthe and crème de cacao in a cookie crust.

articles.title: Canada rejects US terms for trade deal as 50 percent tariffs take effect
articles.summary: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney pulled his country’s negotiators from trade talks with the U.S. on Friday evening, just hours before the Trump administration’s new round of tariffs were set to go into effect. This decision followed weeks of intense negotiations between the two nations over President Trump’s proposed 50 percent tariffs on over $20…
articles.body:
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney pulled his country’s negotiators from trade talks with the U.S. on Friday evening, just hours before the Trump administration’s new round of tariffs were set to go into effect.

This decision followed weeks of intense negotiations between the two nations over President Trump’s proposed 50 percent tariffs on over $20 billion worth of Canadian goods.

These new tariffs — which were originally scheduled to go into effect on Wednesday — would impact a range of goods, including wine, hockey sticks, cement, plywood and more. The prime minister has said these new policies are in “ direct violation ” of the free trade agreement between the U.S., Mexico and Canada.

Carney vowed to “match those tariffs dollar for dollar” in a statement released Friday evening on social media . He added that Canada’s government will present “additional measures” to support workers and business owners in the country in the coming days.

While the prime minister noted Canadian negotiators made “significant progress” in recent weeks, he said this had “not been enough to meet our objectives for Canadians.”

“As a result, this evening, I have decided to suspend trade negotiations with the U.S. and have directed Canada’s negotiators to return to Ottawa,” he said in his statement.

“They have worked hard, in good faith, to defend the interests of Canadians throughout these negotiations up until the very last minute,” Carney continued. “However, last-minute changes in the U.S. proposed terms were unfair, uneconomic, and called into question the reliability of any deal.”

U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer slammed Canada over its decision to walk away from these discussions in a statement shared on his official social media page .

“Despite the U.S. offer to Canada to receive the best treatment of any major exporter to our market, new demands and walk backs of other commitments by Canada have upended the careful balance reached in the past days,” Greer wrote, calling this a “missed opportunity” for a partnership between the two nations.

Canada and the U.S. have historically enjoyed a close relationship, but the Trump administration’s aggressive efforts to broker new trade agreements that favor the U.S. have placed these ties to the test.

Trump has repeatedly suggested that the U.S. cede its northern neighbor as a “51st state” and addressed Carney as the “future governor of Canada.”

Carney wrote that Canada’s negotiators in these tariff discussions have “worked in that context.”

“We have recognized from the beginning that America has changed, and that we will not return to our old relationship,” Carney continued. “Our government understood, before many, that America is altering all its trade relationships. Putting tariffs on its closest allies and charging access for its vast market.”

articles.title: Have You Experienced “Raise Shaming”? Here’s What It Can Look Like at Work
articles.summary: When asking for what you deserve in the office comes with a guilt trip.
articles.body:
When Emma, a project coordinator in Atlanta, found herself tasked with the responsibilities of her boss's job without any of the titles, recognition, or pay that came with it, she started preparing for her next salary negotiation. "I put together this whole proposal comparing market trends, the benefits I've given to the company since I joined, and the points I wanted to make to the director," she said, recounting best negotiation practices she'd learned from years of women in the workplace lunch-and-learns, best-selling business books, and Instagram motivation to 'just ask for more' and 'charge your worth'.

So when the director of her division responded by reminding Emma that she'd already agreed to a $43,000 annual salary when she accepted the job a year earlier, and suggested Emma move back in with her parents or get a second job if she needed to earn more money, she was shocked. "They made this one comment, 'It's like you're asking us to buy you a Louis Vuitton bag,' as if I was asking the company to pay for my life of luxury," said Emma. "I just wanted to be able to afford a dingy 700-square-foot apartment," she added. But her director doubled down: Shouldn't she just be happy with what she already had?

Related: Gen Z Is Making a Surprisingly Smart Retirement Move Right Now

Why Asking for More Can Come With Backlash

This pattern came up in dozens of interviews I conducted with women about their negotiation experiences—raise shaming: Women who spoke up, asked for more, and asserted their value only to be chastised, shamed, or even punished for doing so:

"We're not sure we want someone so money-motivated."

"You're asking for more money? We're a startup."

"It seems like this isn't a good fit for you and good luck finding something else."

For decades, popular career advice for women has rested on the assumption that gender pay gaps, promotion gaps, and leadership gaps were driven by women not negotiating enough. For women like Emma, who grew up on this advice only to find themselves judged, ridiculed, and penalized for asking for 'too much,' the experience can be disorienting, even demoralizing. "I was kind of shell-shocked. I was not expecting to be treated that way," said Emma. "It just made me feel completely devalued."

"Traditional [negotiation] advice assumes that the same words delivered the same way will be received the same way from everyone, and that's not the case," says Damali Peterman, attorney, negotiation expert, and author of Be Who You Are to Get What You Want. "A woman displaying the same behavior as a man could be described as aggressive, demanding, or difficult. A man doing the exact same thing can be described as confident, decisive, or leadership material," she says, pointing to a gendered double standard that not only leads to different perceptions but also to different outcomes.

"A woman displaying the same behavior as a man could be described as aggressive, demanding, or difficult. A man doing the exact same thing can be described as confident, decisive, or leadership material."

Damali Peterman, attorney, negotiation expert, and author

Researchers consistently find that when women express the assertiveness and ambition necessary to be seen as competent or to advance at work, they're not only perceived as less likable than their male peers, they're also perceived as less hireable . When women ask for more, they're not only more likely to be labeled aggressive and demanding, they're more likely than their male counterparts to experience penalties as a result. I interviewed women who were sidelined from future advancement or excluded from existing opportunities; some who even had job offers rescinded after asking for more.

"I think that we as a society have to stop pretending that the only thing that's standing between women and equitable compensation is a willingness to ask," says Peterman. Indeed, more recent research has revealed that women in the U.S. have been as likely to ask for raises and promotions as their male peers for decades , but the judgment levied against women who ask leaves them far less likely to get what they want when they do.

"When I started negotiating my salary, it was very clear that many of my male bosses specifically felt really uncomfortable about it," business journalist and author of Uncompete: Rejecting Competition to Unlock Success, Ruchika T. Malhotra, told me. "I had one male boss who said, 'Yes, you deserve it, but what will our other male reporters think?'"

Even after changing workplaces—a new job, a new manager, and in a new industry—the raise shaming continued. "The most egregious was when I negotiated my salary and my manager basically said that because your husband is in the technology industry (which is high paying), you don't need a raise," said Malhotra. "Hearing that was definitely a slap in the face."

While the message that you get what you ask for (or deserve) might seem empowering, Malhotra points out how it can actually work to disempower those most affected by this bias-driven backlash. "If you come in with this view that the world is meritocratic, like what matters is how good you are, how hard you work and nothing else, when you face this sort of backlash and bias, it can feel very difficult and emotionally unsettling," said Malhotra. "It could very much bring out those feelings of I don't belong here, I'm not good enough, all of that"—conditioning those who already face the most systematic discrimination (across gender identity as well as race, sexuality, ability, and other intersections of identity) to internalize it as a personal failure.

"If you come in with this view that the world is meritocratic, like what matters is how good you are, how hard you work and nothing else, when you face this sort of backlash and bias, it can feel very difficult and emotionally unsettling."

Ruchika T. Malhotra, journalist and author

"Financial shame is such a powerful and complicated thing because it can be something that you did, but it could also be something that happened to you," says Hanna Horvath, Certified Financial Planner and creator of the Your Brain on Money newsletter. "You can internalize that shame whether it's valid or not. And a lot of times it's not valid, and it changes the way that you approach your money and these kinds of decisions going forward," she adds.

Indeed, research affirms that women are given more negative evaluations, are considered less likable and are deemed less worthy of workplace opportunity when they self-promote, and it's this real increase in backlash (as opposed to a lack of confidence) that can keep them from self-promoting to the same extent in the future. In this way, the cost of raise shaming can compound, as those already most exposed to it modify their behavior to shield themselves against more of it.

What to Do If You Experience Raise Shaming

"It's really important that you don't confuse someone else's discomfort with your ambition as evidence that your request was unreasonable," says Peterman . In fact, she encourages women to continue asking for more with these biases in mind, instead of being blindsided by them. To do that, Peterman developed what she refers to as a RESET framework:

Regulate your immediate reaction and take the time to separate the emotional injury of being shamed or penalized from strategic decisions about what you should do next. "Whether it's disappointment, anger, or embarrassment—you should feel all those things," says Peterman. That said, she cautions against shame. "If you ask a legitimate question about compensation, that's not a character flaw," she says.

Examine what actually happened. What changed after the negotiation? Peterman points out that a rejected request for more is not the same thing as being shamed for asking in the first place. "If it's just a 'no,' maybe it's a 'no' to that specific ask," says Peterman, in which case, the rejection can be an opportunity to collect more information. "There's so many different ingredients that can go into that end result—reorganization, acquisition, or merger," in addition to bias, says Peterman. You may want to ask, " Can you help me understand the business reason for that decision?"

That said, if you get a "no" and suddenly find yourself uninvited to meetings, removed from projects, getting drastically different performance feedback and evaluations, excluded from previous advancement opportunities, characterized as difficult or aggressive or ungrateful, or experiencing major changes in bonuses or other compensation, you can use that information to substantiate your experience of backlash.

Save the record to create a factual timeline of what happened and document any specific changes (like those listed above). In addition to creating a contemporaneous record of events, Peterman says this process can help separate the immediate conclusions we come to in the aftermath of such shocks from the documented facts, which can lead to different determinations as we gather further insight or context.

Engage strategically to gather those additional insights, considering who may offer the best and the safest sources of information. It might be a supervisor with whom you have a good relationship, a mentor who you trust, or someone in HR who can offer a more neutral perspective or more insight into what actually drives pay and promotion decisions across the organization.

Take back your power. "It might be to negotiate in a different way or negotiate a more defined path forward. It might be to try to repair the relationship or a misconception. It may be to think about a different workplace that better recognizes that woman negotiator's value," says Peterman.

Peterman also encourages taking back your power in ways that extend beyond the specifics of any one negotiation, like sharing your experience with others, taking classes, or even creating art or pursuing other totally unrelated ventures. "Every time I meet someone who's had a setback, I encourage them to find a way to use that to bounce back so it doesn't have to be a permanent setback," she says.

"Every time I meet someone who's had a setback, I encourage them to find a way to use that to bounce back so it doesn't have to be a permanent setback."

"Strength in numbers is super important," says Malhotra, speaking to the ways in which taking back power and even shifting systems of power in and of themselves can often best be realized collectively rather than individually. "Some of the strongest changes come through solidarity, gathering with other employees, maybe even leveraging ERGs as a place to push for change," she says.

But even at the individual level, Malhotra advocates for building your own personal "board of directors" or "team of champions" that can both cheer you on and provide critical support in the face of workplace cultures that continue to subject some to far more of this backlash than others. This can advance the collective conversation that liberates more of us from internalizing this systemic bias as a personal failure, and puts the shame where it really belongs—on the organizations and institutions that continue to engage in it.

Related: It's 2026—So Why Is Talking About Money Still So Taboo?

articles.title: Gaza is running out of places to bury the dead
articles.summary: Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza has seen thousands of bodies buried in makeshift sites.
articles.body:
Twenty-year-old Omar al-Sawhi has to find a burial place for his father, Mohammad, 40, who was shot dead close to the “Yellow Line”, an Israeli-designated military zone in Gaza.

Mohammad, from the Zeitoun neighbourhood of Gaza City, was working at a small roadside stall selling tea and coffee when a bullet struck him in the neck on June 10, killing him almost instantly.

Omar headed to the Zeitoun Cemetery to bury his father and found the graves tightly packed together, many of them victims of Israel’s ongoing genocide in Gaza.

Many of them are marked with just a stone and a piece of paper attached bearing the name of the deceased, due to a lack of space and the difficult conditions caused by the war.

“I stood in the middle of the cemetery and saw so many graves. There were mountains of sand, with people buried underneath,” Omar told Al Jazeera.

“A grave was just a stone with a piece of paper bearing the name of the martyr, without the grave being built or properly prepared as it was before the war.”

A grave here currently costs about 500 shekels ($167), a sum his family could not afford, so they had to find an alternative.

“There was also no space for a new grave, so we had to bury him in my grandfather’s grave,” he said.

The complete breakdown of services in Gaza and the dangers from Israeli attacks meant that thousands of dead Palestinians have been counted as “missing” during the war.

Many of them were buried in gardens, or tents, or the grounds of camps for the displaced, schools or hospitals.

After a relative reduction in Israeli violence in Gaza following the United States-brokered ceasefire in October 2025, families began to recover their dead loved ones from the debris of destroyed homes or temporary burial sites.

At least 1,200 Palestinians have been killed since the ceasefire was announced, every one of them needing a space for burial. Authorities in Gaza said the remains of 529 Palestinians were recovered from seven mass graves in the grounds of hospitals.

Taking advantage of the brief lull in Israeli violence, his family excavated Mohammad’s remains and moved them to a cemetery for a final burial.

The shortage of graves is not just due to the more than 73,000 Palestinians killed since the war on Gaza began in October 2023, but also the destruction of burial sites by Israel.

According to Gaza’s Ministry of Endowments and Religious Affairs, more than 40 cemeteries have been destroyed since the war began.

Israeli forces have also enforced tight restrictions on access to cemeteries in areas under their control, which has further reduced the number of burial spaces available to families.

With hundreds of thousands of Palestinians forced from their homes by Israeli bombing and forced displacement orders, areas previously designated for burial sites have been converted into shelters for the displaced.

Authorities in Gaza say that shortages of materials, such as headstones, mean the cost of burial now ranges between 700 ($235) and 1,000 shekels ($335).

Masonry from destroyed buildings, mud, or corrugated metal sheets are used as temporary grave markers until the money can be found for a proper gravestone.

Ikrami al-Madallal, a media official at the Endowments Ministry, said many of Gaza’s 60 cemeteries were already at full capacity when the war began.

“We need to establish new cemeteries because of the shortage of available burial space,” he told Al Jazeera.

The ministry is searching for new burial grounds, and transferring bodies from temporary places of rest to cemeteries is an ongoing challenge for authorities.

“The transfer of bodies cannot be carried out randomly. It must be coordinated with the Ministry of Endowments, local government and the relevant government authorities,” he said.

Tafesh Abu Hatab, 50, who has worked as a gravedigger for more than 19 years, said the war on Gaza has been the most difficult period of his career.

Khan Younis Cemetery, where he works, had about 60 graves at the beginning of the war. Now it contains 6,000, and at one stage of the war, Tafesh was preparing about 35 graves a day.

“We have never experienced a period of bloodshed this devastating,” he told Al Jazeera. “Not a day passes without dozens of martyrs being buried.”

Many of the dead he handles are women and children, including infants. Sometimes the bodies of whole families enter the cemetery after an Israeli bomb obliterates an entire building, vehicle, or tent.

“They destroy our homes over our heads, and from the rubble of those homes, we build our graves,” he said.

articles.summary: Fires between January and July burned more than 200,000 hectares of land, says the government.
articles.body:
The Indonesian government is sending 1,500 more soldiers to Borneo to help tackle wildfires that have burned through swaths of the island and created thick smog, choking some areas.

Fires this year have scorched at least 200,000 hectares (495,000 acres) of land – an area three times the size of the capital, Jakarta, the government said – as dry conditions, driven by a powerful El Nino weather pattern, take hold.

list 2 of 3 Wildfires burn across Indonesia as officials cite El Nino as a cause

list 3 of 3 Indonesia closes national park in East Java as wildfire expands

President Prabowo Subianto, on a visit to the region on Saturday, ordered increased troop deployment, Indonesian Cabinet Secretary Teddy Indra Wijaya said.

“An additional three Indonesia National Armed Forces battalions, or around 1,500 personnel, will be brought in from outside Kalimantan starting today,” Teddy said in a statement.

Kalimantan is Indonesia’s part of Borneo, which the country shares with Brunei and Malaysia.

Six helicopters are also being sent to boost waterbombing operations, Teddy said.

The government is monitoring the situation closely and mobilising resources to help contain the spread of the blaze, Prabowo told reporters in the Central Kalimantan provincial capital of Palangkaraya.

“We’re taking mitigation measures. The important thing is to immediately stop the spread of fire spots,” the president said.

Smog from the fires has prompted local governments in Borneo, home to pristine rainforest and vast plantations, to advise residents to wear masks and stay indoors.

The fires have sent smoke into Malaysian Borneo, with six areas of Sarawak state recording “unhealthy” air quality.

The area burned is already larger than during previous El Nino seasons in 2019 and 2023, but not as large as in 2015 during a particularly strong El Nino.

El Nino is a naturally occurring climate phenomenon that brings worldwide changes in winds, air pressure and rainfall patterns. It typically brings drought in Indonesia.

Climate change can amplify its effects because a warmer ocean and atmosphere make more energy and moisture available to feed extreme weather events.

articles.title: Travelers rage as budget airline plans overhead bag fee: 'Highway robbery'
articles.summary: Budget airline passengers will soon have to pay extra money to put their carry-on bags in an overhead bin, and many travelers are already complaining about the extra charges.
articles.body: Jetstar is facing some pushback after announcing its passengers will soon have to pay extra to put their carry-on bags in the overhead bin.  The Australian budget airline, owned by Qantas, will require passengers to pay fees from $25 AUD (about $18) per overhead bag per flight starting in Feb. 2027. The "priority carry-on" purchase will include priority boarding. Passengers will not be charged for a smaller bag, such as a backpack, handbag or laptop bag, that can fit under the seat in front of them. UNRULY PASSENGERS COULD BE BANNED FOR LIFE FROM MULTIPLE AIRLINES UNDER NEW PROPOSAL The updated policy replaces Jetstar’s previous carry-on rules, which allowed passengers to bring carry-on luggage up to a total of 7kg (about 15.4 pounds) aboard. Fox News Digital reached out to Jetstar for comment. In an interview with Fox News Digital, Steven Arroyo, an aviation expert based in Florida and a retired captain for United Airlines, said the new policy can "certainly expedite the boarding process." He also said other airlines may follow suit. "Oil prices have doubled. It's a third of an airline's expense," he said. MAJOR AIRLINE ROASTS PASSENGERS WHO JUMP UP RIGHT AFTER LANDING, IGNITING FIERCE BACKLASH Arroyo said the cost will have an impact on larger families. "If you're traveling with a big family, it's going to [have] impact," he said. "That's going to be the main focus. Will the consumer accept these new fees that airlines are proposing?" Some travelers have not reacted well to the news. MYSTERY WI-FI NETWORK ABOARD FLIGHT RAISES 'UNUSUAL' ALARM ABOUT TRAVELERS' INFORMATION A number of Instagram users responded with pleas to boycott.  "Highway robbery, Jetstar! You think it will be less frustrating being charged for locker space than getting your stuff weighed?" commented an Instagram follower. A second person quipped, "Soon they will also charge to use [the] toilet." The company sees it differently. Stephanie Tully, CEO of Jetstar, positioned the fees as a way to "streamline boarding and help more flights depart on time" while allowing customers to "only pay for what you need," according to a company press release. The company wants to "streamline boarding and help more flights depart on time." Some travelers agreed with the new policy. "Fair enough because it’s annoying when you have a small carry-on, and it has to be put several seats away from you because someone has a larger case," an Instagram user said. On Reddit, a user said the new policy was better "than people trying to sneak in multiple 10kg bags."  CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE STORIES "If we are really lucky, the current carry-on addicts will reconsider," another Reddit user said. Airline insiders said they aren’t surprised by the new charges.  "Jetstar is catching up to a market that got there years ago," Koen Karsbergen, an aviation strategy consultant and educator, told Fox News Digital. Karsbergen said Frontier and Allegiant haven't included overhead bin space in their ticket prices for several years. Arroyo pointed to the now-defunct airline PEOPLExpress.  When PEOPLExpress began selling tickets in the 1980s, the carrier adopted an à la carte pricing model, charging separately for carry-on bags in overhead bins, coffee, tea and bottled water. articles.title: Iran says ‘world approved our victory’ over the US
articles.summary: Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said Friday the war between the U.S. and Iran should end because the world has accepted Tehran’s victory in this conflict. His comments, which were reported by state media, come ahead of new economic sanctions from the U.S. expected next week. “The entire world approved our victory and the U.S. is…
articles.body:
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said Friday the war between the U.S. and Iran should end because the world has accepted Tehran’s victory in this conflict.

His comments, which were reported by state media, come ahead of new economic sanctions from the U.S. expected next week.

“The entire world approved our victory and the U.S. is hated,” he said, according to the state-run IRNA News Agency.

President Trump announced Wednesday that his administration would unleash the “most crushing economic operation ever” against Iran amid ongoing negotiations to reopen the Strait of Hormuz.

“Oil smuggling, swap lines, cash transfers, exchange houses, ship registries, front companies — It all needs to stop NOW. You know who you are,” the president wrote in a Truth Social post.

“This will be an ECONOMIC D-DAY, and we need all of our Allies to stand with the United States of America to isolate, and defeat, the Iran threat,” Trump continued.

The trading passage, which carries around a fifth of the world’s oil consumption on a daily basis during peacetime, has been effectively closed due to Iranian counterstrikes and a U.S. naval blockade.

Iran and Oman have joint jurisdiction over this critical waterway, but Trump has threatened to make the strait a U.S. territory amid these ongoing talks.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent is expected to unveil details of the new economic sanctions on Monday.

“It is a one-two punch. We have ​the blockade, and we are going to have the toughest sanctions in history,” the secretary told ​CNBC on Thursday. “It is going to work in Iran and we are going to collapse this ⁠regime.”

Iranian Foreign Affairs Minister Abbas Araghchi decried these anticipated economic penalties on Thursday, suggesting they were a means for the Trump administration to distract from domestic concerns about the cost of living.

“The so-called “Economic D-Day” is a diversion from America’s own crisis: unprecedented debt & surging interest costs,” the Iranian official wrote on social media . “Doubling down on failed policies will only bring further defeat—and enmity of Iranians. US economic terrorism threatens global economy and sovereignty worldwide.”

articles.title: Carney faces crucial test after calling Trump's bluff
articles.summary: The Canadian prime minister will have to sell his gamble that walking away from talks with the White House will be worth the consequences.
articles.body:
The United States and Canada have entered into uncharted territory.

The longtime allies and economic partners, who have enjoyed free trade for decades, are now in an escalating trade war with no clear off ramp.

And for Prime Minister Mark Carney, the late night decision to suspend talks with President Donald Trump and to retaliate instead of agreeing to a deal that seemed in reach will be a significant political test.

He is one of the first world leaders to walk away from the negotiating table with the White House - and the outcome will be closely watched.

Both sides have blamed last-minute changes for torpedoing the tentative deal, with Carney saying the US "asked too much" and "offered too little".

Carney's decision will challenge the appetite among Canadians to accept some economic pain as Ottawa pushes for more US concessions.

After rejecting Trump's high pressure tactics, and in choosing to hit back against the latest duties, Carney will need to convince Canadians that the economic pain is worth the cost of standing up to the Trump administration in search of a better agreement in the long run.

In remarks on Saturday, he said "we take this step confident this is in the best interest of Canada" and accused the US of a "power play" by seeking eleventh-hour changes.

Asked by a reporter whether the US and Canada were locked in a trade war, he replied: "You're at war when you're attacked - we got attacked."

Switching to French, he said the spiralling trade dispute "wasn't our choice", adding: "Canada is strong, Canada is ready, Canada is united."

There is no doubt this will cause pain on both sides of the border, with business facing more pressure from US duties and Canadian counter-tariffs.

Canada sends about 70% of its exports to the US, and the country is the top trading partner for a number of US states, with Michigan, Kentucky, Indiana and Ohio among the most exposed.

Carney came to power with a call for "elbows up" - an ice-hockey term for an aggressive approach - vowing to fight for Canada in the face of a Trump administration keen to exert economic pressure for its America First agenda.

Many Canadians have told pollsters that they are willing to fight.

A recent survey by Abacus Data suggested that around 36% of Canadians would support retaliating to US tariffs, while a Leger poll indicated that 56% of Canadians want the federal government to take a hard line and make no more concessions.

Canadians frustrated with the US tariffs have already chosen to avoid travelling there. The boycott has meant a loss of about C$3.3bn ($2.35bn; £1.75bn) in travel revenue for the US last year.

A decision by most provinces to remove US alcohol from store shelves has hammered that sector.

Based on US government trade data, US wine exports to Canada fell 78% year over year, a $357m loss in export value. The US distillers association reported similar numbers - saying provincial bans have caused exports of American spirits to drop by more than 70%.

The ban quickly became a point of frustration for the Trump administration.

Canada’s prime minister will also need to convince the provinces who have been less affected by the US trade dispute so far that walking away is a risk worth taking.

He briefed them on Saturday on the current state of affairs, and for now, they are showing a united front.

British Columbia Premier David Eby said he was committed to the "national project we are on", while Ontario Premier Doug Ford said "we didn't start this fight, but I can assure you, we're going to win this fight."

Many Canadians are boycotting the US, so this is where they're travelling instead

Canada says it will match US tariffs 'dollar for dollar' as trade talks break down

Carney calls Trump's fresh tariffs a 'miscalculation' after trade talks collapse

For a week, it seemed that a deal between Washington and Ottawa was in reach.

It's still unclear exactly how the talks fell apart in the final hours, but by all accounts it came down to the wire.

Carney said that late US proposed terms "were unfair, uneconomic, and called into question the reliability of any deal".

He added on Saturday those terms included demands on the automobile sector and "unacceptable" restrictions on trade deals with other countries.

In one biting line, he said of the Trump administration: "We recognise sometimes its signature is written in pencil."

US trade representative Jamieson Greer, meanwhile, pointed to "new demands and walk backs of other commitments by Canada".

In a statement on Friday, the Distilled Spirits Council of the United States suggested "Canadian provinces' continued refusal to return US spirits products to store shelves has led to this outcome".

There were also reports by Canadian media that US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick was unhappy with the deal. The BBC has contacted his office for comment.

And as details on an interim trade agreement with the US trickled out over last week, some provincial leaders, industry groups and political opponents raised concerns that the prime minister had not delivered on the fight he promised - though Carney denied that swayed his thinking.

Ford, usually one of the most vocal Canadian politicians on US tariffs, had been silent on the tentative deal all week. But in a letter sent to Carney, he raised concerns that an agreement under pressure would “embolden the United States to seek concession after concession".

The province, which has a large manufacturing and vehicle sector, has been among the hardest hit regions in this trade dispute.

Conservative opposition leader Pierre Poilievre said that any agreement that included "one-sided" tariffs on Canadian industry would be "a bad deal".

On Saturday, he backed Carney's decision to walk away for now, saying: "Canada cannot accept one-sided tariffs that will de-industrialise our country."

The collapse of this agreement calls into question the future of such talks, including an ongoing review of the US-Mexico-Canada free trade pact.

Now Carney - and Canada - must wait to see how Trump responds.

articles.title: Trump says Canada wants 'benefits' of being US state after trade talks collapse
articles.summary: Canada's PM said he was "reluctantly" announcing retaliatory tariffs and accused the US of starting a trade war.
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump has said Canada wants "the benefits of being a state, without being one" after trade talks between the two countries collapsed late on Friday.

The breakdown of negotiations triggered new 50% US tariffs on a range of Canadian goods. Trump also said American farmers had been charged "massive amounts of Tariffs" for years.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney called the fresh tariffs a "miscalculation" designed to "hurt and divide us".

Carney confirmed he would match Trump's tariffs "dollar-for-dollar" from 8 September, including levies on steel, dairy, appliances and electronics, saying the US and Canada were now in a trade war.

Both countries were optimistic of a deal earlier in the week, but talks fell apart after both sides accused the other of making last-minute changes.

"They asked too much and they offered too little," Carney said on Saturday. "You're at war when you get attacked. We got attacked."

Trump's latest comments echo his repeated references to making Canada the "51st state" of America since returning to office, sparking frustration among its leaders and residents.

The collapse of the trade talks upended a deeply integrated trading relationship with no clear path to resolution.

"We cannot accept what they've offered and we will not give what they've asked," Carney said.

Trump told Fox News on Sunday that the Canadians were "foolish" to engage in a trade war with the US and think they will "actually win".

The new 50% US tariffs will apply to a range of Canadian goods, in addition to existing US tariffs on Canadian steel, aluminium, automobiles and lumber.

They are limited in scope, covering about $20bn (Â£15bn; C$28bn) of imports from Canada, or about 5% in total, including wine, dairy, cement, clothing and hockey equipment.

The prime minister said Canada was retaliating "reluctantly" to protect its interests, with details of counter-measures to be released in the coming days.

Carney faces crucial test after walking away from Trump's deal Published 3 days ago

Carney faces crucial test after walking away from Trump's deal

Leaders of other federal parties in Canada, including the Conservative opposition, voiced support for the prime minister, as have the leaders of some Canadian provinces.

Tariffs - a tax on goods imported from other countries - have been a key component of Trump's trade policy, with the US president arguing that they will boost American manufacturing and create jobs at home.

Critics, however, say tariffs have raised prices for American consumers, and have disrupted and damaged the global economy.

Carney's speech on Saturday was his first address to Canadians after he announced late on Friday night that a deal would not be reached, accusing the US side of making "last-minute changes" that were "unfair" and "uneconomic".

US negotiators, meanwhile, accused Canada of making "new demands and walk backs" on terms which had been previously agreed.

US trade representative Jamieson Greer told Fox News on Saturday that there were no plans to resume talks.

He added that the US had been prepared to cut some of its tariffs on Canada as part of the ill-fated deal.

Carney, however, said the US presented "unacceptable" terms that were too restrictive, including curbing Canada's ability to strike new trade deals with other countries.

He also rejected the assertion that Canada had made last-minute requests: "We clarified what was on offer and were continually disappointed by the answers."

Doug Ford, the leader of Canada's most populous province Ontario, backed Carney and said Trump "can't be trusted".

British Columbia Premier David Eby said the US demand for restrictions on Canada's ability to have other trade deals "would reduce us to the economic equivalent of the 51st state".

"It was never acceptable to Canadians," Eby said.

The Conservative opposition leader Pierre Poilievre also appeared to support Carney, calling the latest US levies "unjustified".

Quebec's premier, Christine FrÃ©chette, warned jobs would likely be lost as a result of the new US tariffs.

"Behind these numbers are real people," she said, vowing to introduce measures to support impacted sectors.

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith, whose oil-rich province has worked to make inroads with the Trump administration, urged both sides to resume talks.

The collapse comes after more than a year of on-again, off-again trade talks, which intensified in recent weeks after a US-imposed deadline to strike a deal or face further tariffs.

The two countries were also engaged in a mandatory review of an existing North American free trade agreement, known as USMCA, with Mexico.

The pact was signed by Trump during his first term to replace the 1994 North American Free Trade Agreement. It underpins $1.6tn (Â£1.2tn) in annual trilateral trade across Canada, the US and Mexico.

Earlier this summer, Canada and Mexico had formally requested for USMCA to be renewed for another 16 years. The US, however, declined to renew it in its current form.

Asked how Friday's trade talk collapse would impact the North American free trade pact, Carney said it was "certainly not good news".

articles.title: Canada announces retaliatory tariffs to begin Sept. 8
articles.summary: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said Saturday morning that the country will enact retaliatory tariffs on the U.S. beginning on Sept. 8 in response to the Trump administration’s new 50 percent tariffs. The prime minister said during a press conference that the country will “match Washington’s new tariffs dollar for dollar in order to protect…
articles.body:
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said Saturday morning that the country will enact retaliatory tariffs on the U.S. beginning on Sept. 8 in response to the Trump administration’s new 50 percent tariffs .

The prime minister said during a press conference that the country will “match Washington’s new tariffs dollar for dollar in order to protect Canadian workers, farmers, families and businesses.”

Carney said his government will release more details about these retaliatory policies in the “coming days” and that the tariffs would apply to goods like steel, dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper and electronics.

He stressed during his morning remarks that the Canadian government “take[s] this step reluctantly.”

“Reluctantly because we recognize that some of these measures will raise costs and reduce choice for Canadians,” Carney said. “Reluctantly because we recognize that some U.S. companies and some U.S. states are innocent bystanders in a dispute that they did not want. Reluctantly because this trade dispute is preventing Canada and America from doing so much good that we could do together.

“But at the same time, we take this step confident that it is in the best interest of Canada,” the prime minister added.

The new U.S. tariffs, which went into effect at midnight, impose a 50 percent tariff on over $20 billion worth of Canadian goods. This impacts a wide range of imported products, from wine to hockey sticks to cement.

In a statement released earlier in the day, Carney announced that he had instructed Canadian negotiators to walk away from these trade negotiations on Friday evening, just hours before the new U.S. policies went into effect.

Carney said he made this decision after U.S. negotiators introduced new terms at the last minute.

U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer pushed back on this characterization of these talks in a statement shared on social media.

“Despite the U.S. offer to Canada to receive the best treatment of any major exporter to our market, new demands and walk backs of other commitments by Canada have upended the careful balance reached in the past days,” he wrote, calling this a “missed opportunity” for an economic partnership between the two countries.

articles.title: ‘Not a small issue’: People deported by US to Liberia face uncertain future
articles.summary: Liberia’s government announced the move on Tuesday, two days before the flight. Politicians say they were not consulted.
articles.body:
Monrovia, Liberia – Samwar Fallah began receiving calls this week from people in the United States seeking information about 20 relatives sent to Liberia, a country none of them is a citizen of.

The families asked the Monrovia-based lawyer to find out where their relatives were taken and what would happen to them. He could not tell them much.

list 2 of 4 Liberia to take 1,200 deportees from the US

list 3 of 4 Liberia’s kush crisis: The hidden trade behind a generation at risk

list 4 of 4 From palava huts to TikTok: How Liberians are preserving their past

He knows the group landed at Roberts International Airport near capital Monrovia on Thursday and was driven away in a bus by Liberian officials. He does not know where they were taken, whether they are free to leave, or what legal status they now hold.

Fallah avoids calling them deportees because the government has not defined their status under Liberian law.

“You cannot relocate a citizen from one country to another without clear information as to why that person has been relocated,” Fallah told Al Jazeera. “Imagine you coming from maybe El Salvador and then you find out you are on a plane to Liberia.”

The group is the first transferred under an arrangement allowing Liberia to receive up to 1,200 people deported from the US over the next 12 months.

The Liberian government announced the move on Tuesday, two days before the flight. Politicians say they were not consulted.

Fallah, assisting the families without charge alongside two US immigration lawyers, said they want to know whether their relatives may settle in Liberia, choose where they can go, or eventually return to the US.

The arrangement involves third-country deportation: sending people to a country other than their country of citizenship. It has raised questions about executive power, sovereignty and the rights of those transferred.

The government said the deportees have not been detained and described the arrangement with the US as humanitarian.

Information Minister Jerolinmek Piah said those transferred would be received as “guests of the Republic”. They are free to leave and may seek asylum, he added.

Piah linked the decision to Liberia’s history as a settlement for free and formerly enslaved Black people from the US and a country whose citizens sought protection abroad during 14 years of civil war.

“Liberia’s gesture is entirely humanitarian and in keeping with the country’s longstanding traditions,” he said.

Piah insisted Liberia would not bear the cost. Accommodation, food and eventual onward travel would be covered by the US government and an international partner organisation, he said.

However, the government has not provided further information about the people who arrived on Thursday. It has not disclosed their full nationalities, where they are being housed, the legal documents under which they entered Liberia, or the identity of the international organisation paying for and managing their stay.

The Reuters news agency on Friday reported that five of those people refused to leave the plane and were instead transported to Equatorial Guinea. Al Jazeera has not verified the report independently.

Justice Minister Natu Oswald Tweh said Liberia reviews each passenger list and may reject anyone. “Most of them are people who had immigration violations and offences,” he said.

But the government has not published its screening criteria or said whether any arrivals had US protection orders preventing their return to their countries.

Al Jazeera found out that most of those deported were nationals of Latin American countries, including Venezuela and Cuba.

But “guests” does not establish a legal status under Liberian law. It remains unclear whether those people entered on temporary permits, whether they can work, or whether they must apply for asylum or residency.

Although Piah said the group was free to leave, officials did not allow journalists to speak with them at the airport. They walked down the aircraft steps, boarded a bus and were driven away under official supervision.

Some of the strongest objections came from politicians who say the arrangement may require legislative approval.

Nimba County Senator Samuel Kogar cited Article 57 of Liberia’s constitution, which empowers the president to conduct foreign affairs and conclude treaties, conventions and similar agreements “with the concurrence of a majority of each House of the Legislature”.

“Was this arrangement brought before both Houses of the Legislature and approved by the required majority?” Kogar asked. “If not, then under what legal authority was this agreement made?”

The government said the arrangement rests on diplomatic notes exchanged on September 4 and September 10 last year.

Third Country Deportation Watch, a project operated by Refugees International and Human Rights First, said the text appeared on the US State Department’s website in March. Most Liberians heard about it only in August.

Representative Anthony F Williams, a member of House committees covering national security, human rights and foreign affairs, rejected the idea that the executive could act alone.

“No agreement that borders on the national security of this country, the sovereignty of the country, can just be entered into by the executive branch alone,” he told Al Jazeera.

The legislature is on a break until October. Williams said he would seek answers on housing, healthcare, screening and Liberia’s authority to detain or remove anyone.

His concerns, he said, were about state capacity, not the arrivals.

Liberia lacks the biometric systems and trained personnel to document as many as 1,200 people moving across counties or porous borders, he said, adding that those fleeing persecution could also be traced by the governments they escaped.

Eddie Jarwolo, executive director of NAYMOTE Partners for Democratic Development, said no published plan showed how Liberia would accommodate the arrivals without further straining public services.

Civil society groups were not consulted, he said. He called for independent monitoring of living conditions, spending and legal compliance.

The government insists Liberia received no payment or diplomatic reward for accepting the transfers. Critics have called for disclosure of the negotiations.

The arrangement emerged amid several US decisions affecting Liberia. On December 9, 2025, the countries signed a five-year, $124m health memorandum. Washington also extended B1/B2 visitor visas for Liberians from 12 to 36 months.

Al Jazeera previously reported that those measures followed Liberia’s agreement to accept Kilmar Abrego Garcia , whose mistaken removal from the US to a Salvadoran prison became a political and legal flashpoint.

The US later sought court permission to send him to Liberia.

Meanwhile, migrant visas for Liberians were halted in January, according to Third Country Deportation Watch, and the US awarded Liberia $5m this year for migration management.

Neither government has publicly established a direct link between the deportation arrangement and the visa move. Jarwolo of NAYMOTE said the two nations should disclose whether visa extension was linked to accepting third-country deportees.

“If they were linked, it would raise serious concerns about Liberia’s negotiating position, national sovereignty and public safety,” he said. “Development assistance should not require Liberia to accept individuals whose backgrounds and legal status have not been transparently disclosed and properly assessed.”

University of Liberia Student Union president William Sando said he learned of the arrangement through Facebook before Piah confirmed it.

“They have not adequately informed the Liberian people,” he said, rejecting the minister’s argument as “disconnected from the current reality”.

Sando wanted the government to disclose where the arrivals will live and whether those who remain may work.

Kogar, the senator, said the questions went beyond an opposition to migration.

“This is not a small issue,” he said. “We are talking about our sovereignty, our laws, our national security, and the responsibility we have to the Liberian people. Where are we, the Liberians?”

articles.title: This El Niño could become 'the largest in living memory', forecasters warn. Americans could feel the effects into 2027.
articles.summary: El Niño's effect will be felt in 2027, making it 'very likely' to replace 2024 as the warmest year on record globally.
articles.body:
The El Niño developing over the Pacific Ocean could be "the largest in living memory," according to the Met Office , the U.K.'s national weather service.

The climate phenomenon, which the Met Office is calling "unprecedented," can boost global temperatures and increase the likelihood of extreme weather. Forecasters said it's likely to become the largest of its kind since the 19th century, adding that 2027 is very likely to replace 2024 as the warmest year on record globally.

El Niño is a periodic warming of sea surface temperatures in the eastern Pacific caused by weakening trade winds. It occurs naturally every two to seven years and tends to last between nine and 12 months.

The Met Office's latest forecasts show a rise of more than 5.4°F (3°C) in equatorial Pacific sea-surface temperatures later this year. A typical El Niño brings warming of 1.8°F to 3.6°F (1°C to 2°C), with 3.6°F (2°C) considered a major event.

"I have never seen a forecast that looks like this," Adam Scaife, a professor at the Met Office, told ITN News . "The strength of El Niño in our forecasts is already at very high levels, even at this early stage.

"It peaks in November, December, and by that stage, it looks very much like it's going to be a record event, the biggest in recent history, the biggest in living memory, and perhaps even the biggest for over a century."

The forecast is consistent with warnings from U.S. forecasters that a historically significant El Niño may be looming. Berkeley Earth , a nonprofit climate research group, found in July that there is a 90% chance tropical Pacific temperatures will exceed all records over about 150 years of observations. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration's Climate Prediction Center told Yahoo News it has classified the 2026 El Niño as ranking "among the largest El Niño events."

The Climate Prediction Center puts the odds at 69% that the event exceeds every El Niño measured since 1950 during the October-through-December stretch, and above 90% that it reaches "very strong" strength this fall and winter. The agency gives it a 97% chance of lasting into early spring 2027.

NOAA's outlook for December through February already shows a clear pattern taking shape, with the impacts of El Niño expected to become more pronounced as winter progresses.

"For the U.S., the impacts of El Niño are most clearly evident from fall through spring," Michelle L'Heureux, a physical scientist at NOAA's Climate Prediction Center, told Yahoo News.

"Generally speaking, El Niño tends to increase the storm track over the southern tier of the United States, increasing the chances of above-average precipitation," she added. "At the same time, because the storm track is shifted southward over the U.S., regions across the northern U.S. tend to be drier. The northern U.S. has the highest chances for above-average temperatures, too."

As it strengthens, El Niño's effects are expected to become increasingly apparent around the world — including in the U.S. Forecasters have predicted that warm summer temperatures, including the hottest July on record , may persist for longer than usual .

Parts of the Northeast were still experiencing hot and humid conditions this week as severe weather swept through the region. On Thursday, storms tore through a beach on Long Island, stranded dozens of people in cars in New Jersey and knocked out power in parts of Delaware's capital, the Associated Press reported.

Mike Lichniak, chief meteorologist at Delaware-area TV station WBOC , warned earlier that morning that rising humidity would push temperatures into the 80s and 90s, with a heat index above 100°F in some areas. Severe thunderstorms and an isolated tornado followed that afternoon and evening.

In NOAA's Climate Prediction Center seasonal temperature outlook for fall 2026, released on Aug. 20, the agency favors above-normal temperatures across nearly the entire country from September through November. The Pacific Northwest, the northern Rockies and parts of coastal Alaska have the highest odds, at 50% to 70%, of a warmer-than-normal season.

Much of the rest of the U.S., including the South, Midwest, Northeast and Florida, also has elevated odds of above-normal temperatures, at 33% to 50%.

The lone exception is a pocket of the Ohio Valley, covering parts of Illinois, Indiana, Kentucky and Missouri, where forecasters see "equal chances" of above-, near- or below-normal temperatures. No part of the country is expected to see a cooler-than-average fall.

The Climate Prediction Center's December-through-February outlook puts the wettest odds over Southern California, the southern tier and much of the East Coast, with its strongest confidence in the Southeast. The drier signal is confined to the northern tier, where the agency also expects above-normal temperatures.

That leaves the northern U.S. warm and dry, which is not the combination that produces heavy snow. The southern storm track can bring it instead to places that rarely get much.

articles.title: Red Lobster brings back Endless Shrimp after promotion helped push chain toward bankruptcy
articles.summary: Red Lobster rebuilt its Endless Shrimp promotion with stronger financial discipline and limited-time pricing after the permanent offer fueled bankruptcy.
articles.body: Red Lobster is once again offering its Endless Shrimp promotion that contributed to millions of dollars in losses before the seafood chain filed for bankruptcy two years ago. The company told Fox News Digital it decided to bring back Endless Shrimp because the promotion still matters enormously to its customers, who "never stopped asking for it." "They continued telling us they missed it, showed up when we brought it back this spring and kept asking for more after that run ended," Red Lobster said. AMERICA'S CHEAPEST POPCORN SHRIMP BASKET AT A CHAIN RESTAURANT COSTS UNDER $9 "We weren’t going to walk away from something they love simply because the previous operating model did not work," the company added. "The better answer was to fix what didn’t work and bring it back in a way that is right for our guests, our restaurant teams and the company." According to Red Lobster, the spring run also proved the company could bring Endless Shrimp back in a way "that delights our guests and works for our restaurant teams and our business." Participating locations began offering the current Endless Shrimp deal for a limited time Aug. 17. "Guests can mix and match five flavors endlessly throughout the meal for as much shrimp as they like, any way they like it," Red Lobster announced in a press release. The lineup includes new garlic bread-crusted shrimp, shrimp linguini Alfredo, garlic shrimp scampi, Parrot Isle coconut shrimp and Walt’s Favorite Shrimp, hand-breaded, butterflied shrimp lightly fried and served with cocktail sauce. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER Red Lobster closed dozens of locations nationwide in May 2024 before filing for Chapter 11 bankruptcy, Fox News previously reported. Many analysts and media reports have cited the company’s decision to make Endless Shrimp a permanent offering as one factor behind its financial troubles. Endless Shrimp returned to select Red Lobster locations in the spring of 2026, but the chain’s 37-year-old CEO, Damola Adamolekun, made it clear in a statement to affiliate FOX 13 Tampa Bay that the promotion would be available for a limited time only. "The previous model did not work, so we did not repeat it," Red Lobster told Fox News Digital. "We rebuilt Endless Shrimp around much stronger operational and financial discipline, including better forecasting, kitchen flow, menu structure and restaurant support.  "We also designed the current offer to work as a dine-in experience, with pricing that can vary by market. The new standard is simple: Endless Shrimp has to work for the guest, the restaurant team and the business." CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS The spring run of Endless Shrimp "met and exceeded our expectations in several important ways," Red Lobster told Fox News Digital. "Guest satisfaction significantly outperformed the average for Red Lobster promotions, restaurant-team support was stronger than it had been in years and our internal team Proud to Serve and Recommend scores both came in above historical levels," the company said.  "Just as importantly, guests continued asking for Endless Shrimp after the promotion ended." In June 2026, Adamolekun said he was planning "the greatest comeback in the history of the restaurant industry." His plan includes streamlining operations, closing underperforming restaurants, increasing engagement with customers and tapping into their nostalgia. One of the biggest lessons Red Lobster said it learned from the previous Endless Shrimp promotion was that "guest demand alone is not enough." TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ The changes to Endless Shrimp are one example of how Red Lobster operates differently today, the company said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "We are focused first on the guest, but that guest focus is backed by greater operational discipline and financial rigor. With Endless Shrimp, we took an experience guests love, addressed what wasn’t working and proved we could deliver it successfully under a stronger model. That same approach is guiding the broader business," Red Lobster said.

articles.title: Erin Patterson: The hotel booking snafu that could free mushroom murderer
articles.summary: A table tennis tournament and a throat lozenge could help Erin Patterson's lawyers overturn her convictions.
articles.body:
Last July, hundreds descended on Australia's Gippsland region from around the country for the most exciting event on the annual table tennis calendar.

But as elite players vied for medals at the national championships, one of the biggest criminal cases in the nation's history - that of mushroom murderer Erin Patterson - was unfolding just a few kilometres away.

This tournament inadvertently became part of a perfect storm which the triple killer's lawyers are now arguing "fatally undermined" the fairness of her trial.

The jury which condemned Patterson to prison were supposed to be isolated - sheltered from the frenzy surrounding the case while they deliberated.

But accommodation shortages in the region, exacerbated by the table tennis competition, meant they shared a hotel with members of the prosecution, a key police witness, and journalists.

Now Patterson's legal team is trying to overturn her convictions on appeal.

"The only proper remedy is... the order for a re-trial," Patterson's barrister Richard Edney said.

When Patterson served her estranged husband's relatives a poisonous mushroom-laced lunch in 2023, killing three and gravely injuring another, she thrust the sleepy Gippsland region into the global spotlight.

The community of Korumburra, where the victims were beloved figures, became shrouded in grief. Leongatha, where Patterson lived, was gripped by shock. And Morwell, host of the lengthy trial, was overwhelmed by journalists, lawyers and spectators - as were towns nearby.

You couldn't walk down the main street without spotting some of the courtroom's stars, or grab a coffee without overhearing chatter about the case.

Mushroom murders and cancer lie: Nine weeks of evidence that gripped a courtroom

'Everyone knows somebody affected': The small towns in shock after mushroom murders

It was this frenzy from which the jury of 12 needed protection, the trial judge decided.

Jurors are required to consider only the evidence presented to them in court, and must only talk about the case among themselves. In Australia, these rules are so strict that discussion with outsiders is forbidden even after a trial wraps up.

To reduce the risk of contamination and the temptation of gossip, Justice Christopher Beale decided the jury should be sequestered once deliberations began - a relatively rare move which meant they would stay in supervised accommodation with little to no contact with the outside world until they reached a decision.

But finding the jury, and the jury keepers watching them, somewhere to sleep became something of a logistical nightmare.

As the trial dragged on, stays became longer than anyone anticipated and accommodation became a constant scramble.

And the week the table tennis tournament came to town - which by a stroke of bad luck was the one in which the jury finally retired - turned the accommodation drought into a famine.

At 08:28 on Monday 7 July, an email from the judge's chambers popped into the inboxes of the lawyers in the case.

It revealed that the lead detective who investigated the murders - a key trial witness - and two prosecution solicitors had been staying at the same hotel as the sequestered jury.

The jurors had exclusive use of a separate floor of the hotel, the email said, and had eaten their meals in a conference room, away from all other guests.

Common areas like the lobby were used by everyone, but the jury keeper who reported the issue said there had been no interaction between his charges and anyone from the prosecution case.

"I understand that there is a shortage of accommodation in the district, but it is obviously undesirable," Justice Beale wrote.

About two hours later, the prosecution responded, admitting they had been aware of the situation for days.

The detective "took steps to avoid common areas from the point that he became aware that [the jurors] were there", their email read.

Upon learning their team would cross over with the jury for a single night, the prosecution had done its best to find other hotels for staff. But they couldn't get alternative rooms for two solicitors, though the email stressed the pair also took steps to avoid any "incidental contact".

However, another missive from the judge's chambers quickly overshadowed the hotel mix-up that same afternoon: the jury had reached their verdicts.

They had found Patterson guilty on all counts.

Patterson's lawyers are now arguing the hotel mix-up amounted to a "fundamental irregularity" which "fatally undermined" the integrity of the verdicts.

"We would describe... it as catastrophic," Patterson's appeal counsel, Edney, told Victoria's Court of Appeal this week.

"What occurred here was an inexplicable and perhaps still unexplained failure in the process."

The defence - which Edney pointed out had been kept in the dark several days longer than anyone else - didn't immediately move for a mistrial last July.

Instead, it twice asked the state's juries commissioner to investigate in the weeks following the verdicts. Both requests were rejected, the barrister said, and the reasons have not been made public.

A year on, there remains a "vacuum of evidence" around what occurred during "the most critical week" of the entire trial, Edney argued.

There is no CCTV from the hotel; no sworn statements from those who were sharing it with the jury - a group which also includes an unknown number of journalists; and nothing to say what happened except the two brief emails sent last July.

There was also at least one media report at the time - raised by Edney this week but rubbished by the prosecution lawyers as "unverified" and "seemingly inaccurate" - that the mix-up had led to "people hiding in doorways to avoid contact" and "skipping breakfast".

"My question is... so what?" Justice Peter Kidd bit back.

In any criminal trial, jurors see other parties all the time - in corridors, or even nearby cafes - but they're under the constant supervision of jury keepers who have sworn to ensure there's no improper communication, he said.

Edney conceded there was "no evidence" that the jurors had communicated with anyone else, but said innocent contact - even just seeing the detective or solicitors - could have resulted in "subconscious influence".

"This was a hotel with windows," Edney said several times - a likely thing for it to have, someone from the judge's bench countered.

Patterson's team cited two cases to support their argument: one in which jurors were discharged when one was offered a throat lozenge by a defendant's relative during a coughing fit, and another in which a retrial was ordered after jurors caught a taxi without being escorted by a jury keeper.

"The system worked as it was intended to work," Director of Public Prosecutions Brendan Kissane KC said.

The jury was constantly supervised, and when a potential problem was identified, steps were immediately taken to prevent it becoming an actual issue.

The jury keeper, the lead detective, and the prosecution all say there was no contact.

"The evidence in this case is that there was no interaction between any other person and the jury," he said.

Other cases the defence pointed to in which jury errors resulted in retrials all had evidence of actual contact, he noted.

Patterson has seven appeal grounds - the others relating to rulings on evidence and alleged unfairness by the prosecution - but this one, by the defence's own admission, is unprecedented.

Just as important as actual interference is the perception of interference, said Edney, quoting the trial judge's own speech as he selected jury members on the very first day of the trial.

"Justice must not only be done, it must be seen to be done."

The trio of judges are now deliberating on Patterson's appeal, as well as an argument by the prosecution that her parole period should be scrapped.

They will announce their decisions at a later date.
